name: Mirelle Catalyst Puzzle
summary: Made-up sample problem. Mirelle catalyst is a fictional layered oxide powder that makes a test dye break down in water about 30 times faster below 41 °C, but has no effect at all above that temperature. The puzzle asks what physical change at 41 °C switches the speed-up off; the answer could help design catalysts that save energy by working at low temperatures. A change in the catalyst's structure has been ruled out, and a model based on a thin layer of bound water is disputed and now being tested.

progress.title: Temperature switch measured and the question stated
progress.description: Repeated runs showed the speed-up vanishing between 40 and 42 °C. The question was fixed as: which physical change, in the catalyst, the dye or the water around them, switches the speed-up off at 41 °C?

progress.title: Reaction rate mapped from 5 to 80 °C in 1-degree steps
progress.description: An automated rig measured the rate at every temperature, with and without the catalyst. An AI system planned the runs and fitted the data. The switch is sharp: it happens within about 1 °C.

links.title: Run plan and fitting code (sample link)

progress.title: Search for a structural change in the catalyst at 41 °C
progress.description: The first idea was that the catalyst's layers shift at 41 °C and close off its active sites. X-ray diffraction patterns taken at 35 °C and 45 °C were identical, so the structure does not change. Do not retry this route without evidence of a change that X-rays cannot detect.

progress.title: A thin layer of bound water causes the switch
progress.description: Simulations suggest that an ordered layer of water on the catalyst holds the dye in the right position to react, and that this layer breaks up at 41 °C. Others argue that the simulated layer breaks up too sharply to be trusted, and no experiment has tested the model yet.

progress.title: Test the bound-water model in heavy water
progress.description: Heavy water forms slightly stronger bonds than ordinary water, so the model predicts that the switch moves up by about 4 °C in heavy water. The measurements are under way. A shift near zero would count against the model.

progress.title: Mechanism confirmed by an independent lab
progress.description: Whichever mechanism survives the tests must be reproduced by a second lab before the puzzle counts as solved.
